Knowledge and the knower:
# Knowledge and the knower
## The core theme
Knowledge and the knower is the core theme. It asks how we know what we know, and how our identity, communities and perspectives shape our knowledge. A perspective is a point of view shaped by experience, culture and values.

## Key ideas
Personal knowledge comes from your own experience; shared knowledge is held by groups. Bias is a tendency that distorts judgement. Certainty is the state of having no doubt; justification is the reason for believing something. Confirmation bias, echo chambers and expertise all affect whom we trust.

## TOK tools
Knowledge questions are open questions about knowledge itself, such as "How do we decide what counts as evidence?". The four elements of the knowledge framework are scope, perspectives, methods and tools, and ethics. A knower is a person who knows.

## Key terms
Perspective: a point of view shaped by experience and values
Shared knowledge: knowledge held by a group
Personal knowledge: knowledge from your own experience
Justification: the reason for believing something
Certainty: having no doubt
Knowledge question: an open question about knowledge itself
Knowledge and technology:
# Knowledge and technology
## The optional theme
Knowledge and technology asks how technology changes what we know and how we know it. Technology can extend our senses, store knowledge and create new knowledge, but can also spread misinformation.

## Key ideas
Algorithms decide what information we see. Big data and artificial intelligence raise questions about whether machines can know. Filter bubbles show us only views that match our own. Digital surveillance raises ethical questions about privacy.

Knowledge and language:
# Knowledge and language
## The optional theme
Knowledge and language asks how language shapes and communicates knowledge. Language allows us to share knowledge but can also mislead.

## Key ideas
The Sapir–Whorf hypothesis states that the language we speak influences how we think. Loaded language carries emotional or value judgements. Translation can lose meaning. Ambiguity is when words have more than one meaning. Technical vocabulary allows precise communication in disciplines.

Knowledge and politics asks how power affects knowledge, and how knowledge affects power. Those in power can shape what is taught, published and believed.

Knowledge and Indigenous societies:
# Knowledge and Indigenous societies
## The optional theme
Knowledge and Indigenous societies asks how Indigenous knowledge is produced, shared and protected. Indigenous knowledge is often passed on orally and through practice, and is closely linked to land and community.

## Key ideas
Traditional ecological knowledge is Indigenous knowledge about the environment built over generations. Oral tradition passes knowledge through stories and songs. Questions include how this knowledge has been dismissed or appropriated, and how it can be respected and protected.

# History
## The area of knowledge
History is the study of the past using evidence. Historians interpret sources to build accounts of what happened and why.

## Key ideas
Historical knowledge is shaped by the evidence that survives, the historian's perspective and the questions asked. Hindsight is understanding an event after it has happened. Revisionism is the reinterpretation of accepted views of the past. Questions include whether history can be objective and who decides which stories are told.

## TOK tools

## Key terms
Historical evidence: sources used to learn about the past
Hindsight: understanding an event after it has happened
Revisionism: reinterpreting accepted views of the past
Objectivity: freedom from personal bias

# The human sciences
## The area of knowledge
The human sciences study human behaviour and societies, and include psychology, economics, sociology and anthropology. They use methods such as experiments, surveys, observation and statistical models.

## Key ideas
Human behaviour is hard to predict because people are complex and respond to being observed (the observer effect). Models simplify reality. Questions include whether the human sciences can be as reliable as the natural sciences, and how values affect research.

Human sciences: disciplines studying human behaviour
Observer effect: people changing behaviour when observed
Model: a simplified representation of reality

The natural sciences:
# The natural sciences
## The area of knowledge
The natural sciences study the physical world through observation and experiment. The scientific method involves forming hypotheses, testing them and revising theories.

## Key ideas
A hypothesis is a testable prediction. Falsifiability is Popper's idea that a scientific claim must be capable of being proven false. A paradigm shift, from Kuhn, is a fundamental change in scientific thinking, such as from Newtonian to Einsteinian physics. Peer review checks research before publication.

## Key terms
Scientific method: forming and testing hypotheses
Falsifiability: the possibility of a claim being proven false
Paradigm shift: a fundamental change in scientific thinking
Peer review: experts checking research before publication

# Mathematics
## The area of knowledge
Mathematics is the study of quantity, structure, space and change, built through logical proof. Its knowledge is often seen as certain because it is deduced from axioms.

## Key ideas
An axiom is a statement accepted without proof as a starting point. A proof is a logical argument showing a statement is true. A conjecture is a statement believed true but not yet proven. Questions include whether mathematics is discovered or invented, and why it describes the world so well.

## TOK tools

Proof: a logical argument showing a statement is true
Conjecture: a statement believed true but not proven
Deduction: reasoning from general principles to conclusions

TOK exhibition:
# TOK exhibition
## The exhibition
The TOK exhibition is the internal assessment. You choose one of 35 IA prompts and select three objects that show how TOK manifests in the world. You write a commentary of up to 950 words explaining each object's link to the prompt.

## Doing it well
Choose specific, real-world objects with a personal or local connection. Explain clearly how each object links to the prompt, using evidence and TOK concepts. Justify why each object was chosen. Link all three objects to the same prompt and to the core theme or an optional theme.

## Key terms
IA prompt: one of the 35 prompts for the exhibition
Object: a real-world item used in the exhibition
Commentary: the written explanation of each object
Real-world context: a link to actual events or situations
TOK essay on a prescribed title:
# TOK essay on a prescribed title
## The essay
The TOK essay is a 1600-word essay on one of six prescribed titles released by the IB. It is externally assessed. A prescribed title is a question set by the IB for the essay.

## Doing it well
Unpack the title by defining key terms and identifying the knowledge question. Develop arguments from two areas of knowledge, each with specific real-life examples. Consider counterclaims, the arguments against your claims, and evaluate them. Reach a conclusion that answers the title and explains its implications. A claim is a statement you argue for.

## Key terms
Prescribed title: a question set by the IB for the essay
Claim: a statement you argue for
Counterclaim: an argument against your claim
Area of knowledge: a field such as history, mathematics or the arts
Implication: what follows from your conclusion
